title: Ranking likelihoods fast
objectives: Rank three events by probability within seconds, using benchmarks rather than exact sums.

screens.prose: Trader batteries are reported to include a section on ranking events by likelihood, at a few seconds an event. Rank these three without working anything out on paper.

rows: Exactly 5 heads in 10 flips of a fair coin
A total of 7 with two dice
An ace or a king, one card from a full deck

screens.question: Put the events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: Exactly 5 heads in 10 flips of a fair coin
A total of 7 with two dice
An ace or a king, one card from a full deck

hints.text: Which one is close to a quarter?
A total of 7 is $\tfrac16$; an ace or a king is $\tfrac{8}{52} = \tfrac{2}{13}$.
Five heads in ten is $\tfrac{252}{1024}$, about 0.25: first. Then $\tfrac16$ above $\tfrac{2}{13}$.

feedback.correct: Five heads, then a total of 7, then an ace or a king.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put a rough number on each, then compare.

byKey.t7: A total of 7 is $\tfrac16 \approx 0.167$. Five heads in ten is $\tfrac{252}{1024}$, about a quarter.
byKey.ak: An ace or a king is $\tfrac{2}{13} \approx 0.154$, just below $\tfrac16$.
byKey.h5: Five heads in ten feels rare, but 252 of the 1,024 sequences give it: about 0.25.

explain.text: Five heads in ten is $\tfrac{63}{256} = 0.246$, far ahead. A total of 7 is $\tfrac16 = 0.167$ and an ace or a king $\tfrac{2}{13} = 0.154$. Only that close pair needs a check: cross multiply, 13 against 12.

screens.prose: Make $n$ tries, each with chance $\tfrac1n$, such as six rolls of a die for a six. The points show the chance of no success and of at least one. Slide $n$.

derive.caption: {{n}} tries at 1/{{n}}: none {{fixed(pow(1 - 1 / n, n), 3)}}, at least one {{fixed(1 - pow(1 - 1 / n, n), 3)}}

screens.question: Slide $n$ up to 50. What value does the chance of no success settle near?

hints.text: Watch the point labelled none as $n$ grows.
At $n = 6$ it reads 0.335.
It creeps up towards 0.368, which is $1/e$.

feedback.correct: It settles near 0.37, which is $1/e$; at least one settles near 0.63.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the caption at $n = 50$.

byKey.certain: You expected $n$ tries at $\tfrac1n$ to make a success certain. Read the caption: no success keeps a chance near 0.37.
byKey.half: It never reaches a half. At $n = 50$ it reads 0.364, heading for 0.368.

explain.text: No success settles near $1/e = 0.368$ and at least one near $1 - 1/e = 0.632$. Six rolls already give 0.335 and 0.665. These two numbers are worth knowing by heart.

canvas.caption: Large n: none 0.368, at least one 0.632

screens.prose: A number you know by heart is a **benchmark**: $\tfrac12$, $1/e$ and $1 - 1/e$. Others: 23 people make a shared birthday an even bet; 68% and 95% lie within one and two sds. Place each event against one.
screens.question: Put the events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: At least one six in six rolls of a die

hints.text: Which benchmark does each event sit beside?
Six rolls at $\tfrac16$ is $n$ tries at $\tfrac1n$: near $1 - 1/e$.
30 people is well past 23: about 0.71. Six rolls: about 0.67. Six or more heads: under a half.

feedback.correct: Birthday among 30, then six in six rolls, then 6 or more heads.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Place each event beside a benchmark first.

byKey.six: Six rolls at $\tfrac16$ sit just above $1 - 1/e$: 0.665. Thirty people is well past 23: 0.706.
byKey.heads: Six or more heads is under a half: exactly 5 takes a quarter and the rest splits evenly.
byKey.bday: Thirty people is past the 23 that make an even bet, so above a half: 0.706.

explain.text: Thirty people is well past 23, so the birthday chance is well above a half: 0.706. Six rolls sit a little above $1 - 1/e$: 0.665. Six or more heads is $(1 - 0.246) \div 2 = 0.377$ by symmetry.

screens.prose: All three sit near $\tfrac12$. Say so first: a test that asks for intervals rewards that alone. Then work just enough to separate them. The line is zoomed in round a half.
screens.question: Put the events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: At least one six in four rolls of a die
At least one double six in 24 rolls of two dice

hints.text: Birthday 23 is the benchmark itself: just over a half.
$(35/36)^{24} \approx e^{-24/36} = e^{-2/3} \approx 0.51$, so 24 rolls give about 0.49.

feedback.correct: Four rolls 0.518, then 23 people 0.507, then 24 double-six rolls 0.491.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the two dice events; the birthday is the benchmark.

byKey.b23: 23 people give 0.507. Four rolls give $1 - \tfrac{625}{1296} = 0.518$, a little more.
byKey.dbl: 24 rolls at $\tfrac{1}{36}$ is $np = \tfrac23$, so about $1 - e^{-2/3} \approx 0.49$: below a half.
byKey.four: Four rolls give $1 - \tfrac{625}{1296} = 0.518$, the largest of the three.

explain.text: Four rolls give $1 - \tfrac{625}{1296} = 0.518$, 23 people 0.507, and 24 double-six rolls 0.491. All three lie within 0.02 of a half. Saying that first is worth more than the order.

screens.prose: A count of many flips is close to normal. For 100 fair flips the mean is 50 and the sd is $\sqrt{100 \times \tfrac12 \times \tfrac12} = 5$. Use the 68% and 95% benchmarks.
screens.question: Which is nearest the chance of 60 or more heads in 100 flips?

options.why: 5% lies beyond two sds on both sides together. Only the upper tail counts: about half of that.
You used $\sqrt{100} = 10$ as the sd. It is $\sqrt{100 \times \tfrac12 \times \tfrac12} = 5$, so 60 is two sds up.
You divided by the variance, 25, instead of the sd, 5.

hints.text: How many sds above 50 is 60?
Two sds. The 95% band leaves 5% outside it, split between two tails.
About 2.5%, a little more for 60 itself: about 0.03.

feedback.correct: About 0.03: two sds up leaves about 2.5% in the upper tail.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count sds from 50, then use the 95% benchmark.

byKey.five: 5% lies beyond two sds on both sides together. Only the upper tail counts: about half of that.
byKey.sixteen: You used $\sqrt{100} = 10$ as the sd. It is $\sqrt{100 \times \tfrac12 \times \tfrac12} = 5$, so 60 is two sds up.
byKey.variance: You divided by the variance, 25, instead of the sd, 5.

explain.text: 60 is two sds above 50, and 95% within two sds leaves 2.5% in each tail. With the continuity step, $z = (59.5 - 50) / 5 = 1.9$ gives about 0.029. The exact chance is 0.0284.

screens.prose: Ranking papers sometimes offer “the same” as an option. Ten flips of a fair coin.
screens.question: Which is more likely: exactly 4 heads, or exactly 6?

options.why: Fewer heads is not less likely here. Swapping heads and tails turns every 4-head sequence into a 6-head one.
More heads is not more likely with a fair coin. Each 6-head sequence flips to a 4-head one.
No working is needed: swap heads and tails and the events trade places. Both are $\tfrac{210}{1024}$.

hints.text: Swap the words heads and tails.
Each 4-head sequence is a 6-tail sequence.
So both counts are $\binom{10}{4} = \binom{10}{6} = 210$.

feedback.correct: The same: 4 and 6 mirror each other about 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think of what happens if you swap heads and tails.

byKey.four: Fewer heads is not less likely here. Swapping heads and tails turns every 4-head sequence into a 6-head one.
byKey.six: More heads is not more likely with a fair coin. Each 6-head sequence flips to a 4-head one.
byKey.work: No working is needed: swap heads and tails and the events trade places. Both are $\tfrac{210}{1024}$.

explain.text: Swapping heads and tails maps every 4-head sequence to a 6-head one. So the counts match: $\binom{10}{4} = \binom{10}{6} = 210$ of 1,024. Spot symmetry before you compute anything.

screens.prose: A colleague ranks “at least one six in six rolls” above a shared birthday among 30. Their reason: $6 \times \tfrac16 = 1$, so the six is certain.
screens.question: What is the chance of at least one six in six rolls, to two decimal places?

options.why: You multiplied $6 \times \tfrac16$. That adds the overlaps: a run with two sixes counts twice.
That is the chance of no six, $(5/6)^6 = 0.335$. Take it from 1.
$\tfrac56$ is one roll’s chance of no six. Six rolls must all miss.

hints.text: Find the chance that every roll misses.

feedback.correct: 0.67: one minus the chance that all six rolls miss.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the chance of no six, then take it from 1.

byKey.np: You multiplied $6 \times \tfrac16$. That adds the overlaps: a run with two sixes counts twice.
byKey.none: That is the chance of no six, $(5/6)^6 = 0.335$. Take it from 1.
byKey.oneroll: $\tfrac56$ is one roll’s chance of no six. Six rolls must all miss.

explain.text: Adding $\tfrac16$ six times counts rolls with two or more sixes more than once. No six has chance $(5/6)^6 = 0.335$, so at least one is 0.665. It ranks below the birthday chance among 30, 0.706.

screens.prose: You placed each event against a benchmark, then worked out only the close ones. For $n$ tries at chance $p$, $$P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - (1 - p)^n \approx 1 - e^{-np}.$$ With $np = 1$ that is about $1 - 1/e = 0.63$.
screens.question: What is the chance of at least one success in 10 tries at $\tfrac1{10}$ each?

hints.text: Here $np = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the chance of no success from 1.

byKey.np: $10 \times \tfrac1{10} = 1$ adds the overlaps. The chance is $1 - 0.9^{10} = 0.651$.
byKey.none: 0.349 is the chance of no success. At least one is $1 - 0.349 = 0.651$.

explain.text: No success is $0.9^{10} = 0.349$, so at least one is 0.651. With $np = 1$ every such event sits near 0.63. Fewer tries at a bigger chance land slightly higher.

screens.prose: Why does $n$ tries at $\tfrac1n$ settle at $1/e$? Put the lines in order. Leave out the step that throws away terms that matter.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: Take logs: $\ln\left(1 - \tfrac1n\right)^n = n \ln\left(1 - \tfrac1n\right)$, since a power comes down
For small $x$, $\ln(1 - x) \approx -x$, the tangent line at $x = 0$
Take the complement: at least one success $\approx 1 - e^{-1} = 0.632$

lines.why: Two terms of the expansion work only when $np$ is small. Here $np = 1$, so the dropped terms matter.

hints.text: Start by turning the power into a product.
Logs first, then the small-$x$ step, then undo the log.
s1, s2, s3, s4, s5; leave out the expansion.

feedback.correct: Logs, the tangent step, $-1$, then $e^{-1}$ and its complement.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bring the power down before you approximate.

byKey.d1: Two terms of the expansion work only when $np$ is small. Here $np = 1$, so the dropped terms matter.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the two-term expansion belongs.
byKey.s2: The tangent step comes after the logs, which bring the power down.
byKey.s3: Substitute $x = \tfrac1n$ once the tangent line is in place.
byKey.s4: Undo the log only after the product has become $-1$.
byKey.s5: The complement comes last, from no success to at least one.

explain.text: Logs turn the power into $n$ times a log, which the tangent line makes $-1$. Undoing the log gives $e^{-1}$. The two-term expansion is the $n \times p$ trap in disguise.

screens.title: Ranking in code
screens.prose: `at_least_one(p, n)` returns the chance of at least one success in `n` tries at chance `p`, as an exact `Fraction`. `rank(events)` takes a dict of names to exact chances and returns groups of names, most likely first. Equal chances share a group, names in alphabetical order.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.starter:
from fractions import Fraction


def at_least_one(p, n):
    p = Fraction(p)
    # one minus the chance that all n tries fail
    ...


def rank(events):
    groups = []
    # most likely first; equal chances share a group, names sorted
    ...
    return groups

examples.call: rank({'seven': Fraction(1, 6), 'ace or king': Fraction(2, 13), 'five heads': Fraction(63, 256)})

tests.call: rank({'seven': Fraction(1, 6), 'ace or king': Fraction(2, 13), 'five heads': Fraction(63, 256)})
rank({'six heads': Fraction(210, 1024), 'four heads': Fraction(105, 512), 'seven': Fraction(1, 6)})

tests.setup:
from math import prod
b23 = 1 - prod(Fraction(365 - i, 365) for i in range(23))
tests.call: rank({'birthday 23': b23, 'four rolls': at_least_one(Fraction(1, 6), 4), 'double six 24': at_least_one(Fraction(1, 36), 24)})

widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests, compared exactly. Six are chances as `Fraction`s; five are rankings, one with a tie and one of the close trio.

hints.text: No success in `n` tries has chance `(1 - p) ** n`.
For `rank`, sort the distinct chances from largest to smallest.
For each chance, collect the sorted names that have it: one group.

feedback.correct: Both functions rank the lesson’s events, ties included.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the chances exact, and group equal ones.

explain.text: `Fraction(210, 1024)` and `Fraction(105, 512)` are the same number, so the tie is found exactly. Floats could split it on a rounding error. Sorting the distinct values once keeps the groups in order.

screens.prose: A trader battery’s ranking paper is reported as about 10 items in 10 minutes. This one is from a market-making desk. Place each event against a benchmark first.
screens.question: Put the events in order, most likely first.

lines.text: A quote is hit at least once in 10 seconds, at chance 1/10 each second
At least one of 20 independent trades loses, each with chance 5%
A share whose daily return is normal, mean 0 and sd 1%, falls more than 2% tomorrow

hints.text: Two events have $np = 1$.
Both sit near $1 - 1/e$; the fall is two sds, one tail: about 2.3%.

feedback.correct: The quote, then the trades, then the fall: 0.651, 0.642 and 0.023.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the benchmark for each, then split the close pair.

byKey.trades: 20 tries at 5% sit near $1 - 1/e$: $1 - 0.95^{20} = 0.642$. The quote is $1 - 0.9^{10} = 0.651$, a little more.
byKey.fall: A fall of two sds is one tail beyond the 95% band: about 2.3%, the least likely.

explain.text: Both at-least-one events have $np = 1$, so both sit near 0.63: 0.651 and 0.642. With the same $np$, fewer tries at a bigger chance give slightly more. A 2-sd fall is about 0.023, far below.

ideas: Place each event against a benchmark: $\tfrac12$, $1/e = 0.37$, $1 - 1/e = 0.63$, 23 people for a shared birthday, 68% and 95%.
Work out exactly only the pair that is close; spot ties by symmetry before computing.
At least one success in $n$ tries at $p$ is $1 - (1 - p)^n \approx 1 - e^{-np}$, never $np$.
summary.trap: $6 \times \tfrac16 = 1$ does not make a six certain: it counts rolls with two sixes twice.

quiz.prose: Exactly 5 heads in 10 flips can happen in 252 ways. A total of 7 with two dice can happen in 6 ways.
quiz.question: Which is more likely, and by roughly how much?

options.why: You compared ways without dividing by the totals, 1,024 and 36.
7 is the likeliest total of two dice, but $\tfrac16$ is below $\tfrac{252}{1024}$.
$\tfrac{252}{1024} = 0.246$ is half as much again as $\tfrac16 = 0.167$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide each count of ways by its total first.

byKey.forty-two: You compared ways without dividing by the totals, 1,024 and 36.
byKey.seven: 7 is the likeliest total of two dice, but $\tfrac16$ is below $\tfrac{252}{1024}$.
byKey.same: $\tfrac{252}{1024} = 0.246$ is half as much again as $\tfrac16 = 0.167$.

explain.text: Ways only compare inside one sample space. Divide each by its total: $\tfrac{252}{1024} = 0.246$ and $\tfrac{6}{36} = 0.167$. Five heads wins, by about half as much again.

quiz.question: Roughly what is the chance of at least one six?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the chance of no six from 1.

byKey.np: $12 \times \tfrac16 = 2$ is not a probability. Take $(5/6)^{12} = 0.112$ from 1.
byKey.none: 0.112 is the chance of no six. At least one is 0.888.

explain.text: Here $np = 2$, so the benchmark is $1 - e^{-2} = 0.865$. Exactly, $(5/6)^{12} = 0.112$ and at least one is 0.888. Either is good enough to rank against most events.

quiz.prose: A share’s daily return is normal with mean 0 and sd 1.5%.
quiz.question: Roughly how likely is a move of more than 3% either way tomorrow?

options.why: 2.5% is one tail. Either way counts both tails: about 5%.
32% lies beyond one sd. 3% is two sds of 1.5%.
16% is one tail beyond one sd. 3% is two sds.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count sds, then use the 95% benchmark.

byKey.half: 2.5% is one tail. Either way counts both tails: about 5%.
byKey.third: 32% lies beyond one sd. 3% is two sds of 1.5%.
byKey.sixteen: 16% is one tail beyond one sd. 3% is two sds.

explain.text: 3% is two sds of 1.5%. 95% of days lie within two sds, so about 5% move further either way. The exact value is 4.6%.

quiz.prose: Eight flips of a fair coin. A: exactly 3 heads. B: exactly 5 heads.
quiz.question: Which is more likely?

options.why: Fewer heads is not less likely here: swap heads and tails and A becomes B.
More heads is not more likely with a fair coin: swap heads and tails.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Swap heads and tails.

byKey.a: Fewer heads is not less likely here: swap heads and tails and A becomes B.
byKey.b: More heads is not more likely with a fair coin: swap heads and tails.

explain.text: Exactly 3 heads is exactly 5 tails, and a fair coin treats heads and tails alike. So both have $\binom83 = 56$ of 256 sequences. A test that offers “the same” is often testing this.
